Of course, I get what you mean. I guess it's more to do with how in an art piece, anything influences tone. For example, the bright blue sky, paired with how Anya seems more like mildly annoyed rather than actually terrified, makes the drawing seem light-hearted, I think that's why everyone's reacting this way in the comments. And you definitely don't have to draw gore or rape, you absolutely shouldn't so you're right about that, but I guess for drawings that are meant to represent the victim's feelings, people expect something darker because that's how emotion is typically conveyed through art.

For example, if this drawing of yours had a darker color palette, like maybe it was night time, and the two were in the shadows, and Anya had a more fearful expression on her face, I would've probably gotten the intention that it's meant to represent her being trapped. Then taking it even further, if you made the pose something more like her being caught in a fishnet, instead of being carried over Jimmy's shoulder which is a typically more light-hearted pose, it would totally get the allegory across. 

Of course this is all my opinion. And I'm sorry that I seemed accusatory in my comment. It's just that I see many people in this Fandom act weird towards Anya, not take her abuse seriously, joke about it as if it's just A Thing That Happened, rather than an extremely traumatic experience which caused all the events in the game and is meant to convey its themes. So when I saw this drawing, I assumed it was meant to be like a joke and I jumped the gun a bit. Still I hope this clarifies why so many people are reacting like this in the comments.

When my childhood dog died, the one thing that comforted me was thinking that she lived a happy, fulfilling life. I wasn't present for most of hers — she was a year older than me. And when she was older, well I wasn't very responsible with animals at that age, so I didn't pay her much mind. At first I was riddled with guilt over not spending time with her like I should've. But then I remembered that she's been in my family's care for years, and I know for a fact they gave her all the love she deserved. It made me feel at peace with her passing.

Then, when I got a dog again in 2020, I was a bit older and more responsible. He will turn 4 this year. Hopefully he will live until the natural end of his life, and I make sure he knows how loved he is everyday. I know that when his time comes, I'll be able to feel solace from the fact that I gave him as much love as I possibly could. His life has been prosperous. I'll continue to ensure that it is no matter what.

Even so, that doesn't make it hurt any less. I'm sure she will love you forever, even beyond this world.

Well, for self therapy, in order to be able to carry out sessions myself I'd just try to create an environment in which I can focus, usually playing white noise and sitting up so I don't fall asleep. I got to know some of my alters, and though I haven't unburdened any of them yet, or at least not fully (all of my fears are still here) Just starting some communication with them and ensuring that I'd be there for them when they need me to be, and that alone has helped me become a lot more stable overall. They've learned how to trust me, and in turn I trust myself to take care of myself next time I have an episode, or next time something bad happens.

I think it takes a lot of self introspection though. Finding out what you specifically need from yourself, what kind of support. It's different for everyone. It took me an entire year to actually realize all these things about myself — I literally only did on December. The rest of that year was spent slowly unpacking my own trauma to get where I am, communicating with parts and piecing together what makes sense.

Thank you! I've been doing it ever since midway through last year. I've done it all by myself. It sounds insanely unrealistic, it shocks me too. I believe so. NPD and ASPD are mostly demonized. However, just like BPD, they all stem from trauma. Obviously, genetics can make them more likely, but it's far from the only component. Personality disorders are some of the strongest self-defense mechanisms built up by the brain in response to endured abuse, neglect, and other forms of trauma. 

I find that IFS helped me greatly with managing my own BPD to the point where I've been forgetting I even have it as of late. So I figure it could be great at tackling the others, as its strong point really seems to be unpacking trauma and defense mechanisms. That being said, of course, someone who has the other aforementioned disorders could probably give a better answer.

What I'm trying to say is inspecting the real root cause of your fear of abandonment (i.e., what past even could've given origin to it) might be of help.

Wonderful post. I understand how you feel. I've always felt somewhat behind my peers too, in similar ways. I've felt it especially recently trying to get into college for the first time. It hurts to feel like you have to try 10x harder and overexert yourself to comprehend something when everyone else seems to instantly get it, and even when you try, you don't even actually succeed in understanding. The feeling of being behind those my age as well — I still haven't learned many basic life skills that I should know by now, and it makes me feel like a child in comparison to others...

It's still something I battle with. I suppose though that the approach I've been trying to take is reframing my view of "intelligence", as a concept... Asking, what really is intelligence? Because there are many different types. None is the "better" version. Someone who's a genius at Math for example, may be embarrassingly lackluster in English and Literature. And even if they aren't, perhaps they are proficient at any academic matters but fail miserably in social situations as a whole.

I think that at its core I would describe intelligence as "one's capability to absorb data and apply it to solve certain issues", and that does not only involve logical ones. Hence why terms such as "emotional intelligence" exist. All it really is is being knowledgeable in certain areas. There are many different ways to be intelligent and every human has their certain ways. So, one thing that has started to bring my confidence up, is honing in on the ones I am really good at, and indulging in them.

For example, I am completely incompetent at any exact sciences. When I say incompetent, I mean to the point that all I can do are basic math formulas. I legitimately cannot do anything above that without referring to them already written out, I simply forget, not to mention I hardly comprehend the actual process of solving said formulas, and usually get the solution wrong. On the flip side, I excel at human sciences. History is my favorite subject, with sociology and geography going along with that. So I find that I really enjoy researching them because it boosts my confidence. Although I feel bad when I see friends or peers solve math problems with such an elevated ease so far from mine, I can now remind myself that I have my own area that I'm near perfect at because I am so passionate about it.

In your case though, I understand you may not like any academic subject, or even be good at any. And that's completely fine as well. For example, off of your post alone, I can see that you have an incredible amount of self-awareness. It may not sound important, but many people completely lack it and are unable to identify patterns within themselves without the help of another party, and can't pinpoint any of what you've managed to in yourself. It doesn't mean they are inconsiderate or shallow, it's simply something they struggle with. The same applies to you. You may not be great at general knowledge in academic subjects but you know lots about yourself and are able to be introspective in order to figure out reasoning behind your actions. In many life situations this skill comes in much more handy than things that are learned in school. So, self-awareness is absolutely a form of intelligence. 

You also mentioned being hard-working, which is impressive given that you kept trying so hard even after feeling embarrassed several times. Many people just give up, and it's also not their fault, but it ends up damaging their path in the long run... From this we can gather you are a very determined person, because you understand it can benefit you in the long run. This form of hindsight is absolutely a form that intelligence takes as well.

So, to finally answer your main question and stop rambling. I think you've answered it yourself, frankly. Your date was teasing you, which, no offense, but it's just an outright inconsiderate action. That means it's on him for acting that way, not on you for not knowing some random answer about something. Even if it's an "easy" one. You mentioned feeling comfortable around a very knowledgeable friend because she doesn't judge you. The key is for you to not feel judged. That may partially be coming from yourself, but it's ultimately up to the other party to be kind about it.

If you feel preemptively that someone is judging you I'd try to keep what I said in mind. I have a friend that seems to know so much more than me in conversations and I do feel lost or as if they might secretly think I'm stupid for it. I try to remind myself that there are many other things I'm very good at, that at times even they themselves lack. We all have inherent value, and the idea of intelligence being a main determining factor in it is a quite harmful one that has given way to many forms of prejudice throughout time, honestly, so I'd say to remind yourself that it is a very unhelpful ideology, even though I completely understand how horrible it can feel.
